explanations.explanation: This neuron fires on the very first, headline‐style token of a content block—i.e. the capitalized lead word of a title or introductory sentence marking a new section.

This feature appears to be a detector for closed-class “linker” words—copulas (is/was), auxiliaries (has, been), prepositions (on, by, since), conjunctions/conditionals (or, and, if), and negators (not, haven’t)—that stitch together metadata and boilerplate or scaffolding text (dates, view counts, forum notices, placeholder pages, etc.).
This feature fires on the “dot” that ends sentences, headings, list markers or abbreviations—i.e. the period token signaling a boundary/terminal punctuation.

This neuron fires on the “.” dot when it’s used as a punctuation marker in abbreviations (e.g. “Gov.”, “Inc.”), decimal numbers (e.g. “5.7”, “6.4”), version tags and similar dotted constructs rather than as a generic sentence end.
This feature detects English subordinating conjunctions—words like “if,” “because,” “while,” “although/though,” etc.—that introduce dependent clauses expressing conditions, reasons or contrasts.
This neuron lights up on “if…then” style conditional prompts—especially the “If X**, then Y” clauses that usher in advice, options or calls-to-action in how-to, marketing or instructional text.
This neuron detects the sentence-final full stop – in other words, the period that marks the end of a declarative statement or title. It lights up on the “.” closing off each line.
This feature detects explicit definitional or explanatory cues—verbs like “means,” “symbolizes,” “covers,” “knows,” or “say” that signal the text is giving a definition or gloss of a term or concept.

This neuron consistently fires on high‐level discourse signposts—especially interrogative cues (“Why,” “What,” “Is,” “Think”) and gerundive subwords of verbs used as section‐heading labels (“standing” in Understanding, “Deciding,” “Determining,” “Makes,” etc.)—marking the start of questions or explanatory/decision‐making sections.

This feature fires on the first word of a new section or list item—often a capitalized heading or imperative/prepositional opener that signals the start of a bullet point, recipe step, product call-out or similar content block.
